title: Raga kirtan today
hookLine: the raga name at the top of each hymn is like a recipe card, and teachers and ragis still cook from it, alongside simpler tunes

lines: A RECIPE CARD, SOFT AT THE CORNERS.
THE CARD ALONE CAN'T MAKE THE DISH.
cards: A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. The measurements are vague: a handful, enough, until it smells right. The card alone can't make the dish; somebody has to have stood next to her at the stove.

And yet as long as someone keeps cooking from it, the card stays alive. For weeks, every hymn on this path has come with a raga name at the top, like the title on that card. Today: who is still cooking from it.

teach.b: The Granth gathers its hymns under raga headings: Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, and on through Kalyan, Prabhati and Jaijavanti. The heading tells the singer the musical mode.
The text doesn't write out a melody note by note; like the grandmother's card, it names the dish and trusts that someone knows how to cook it. That knowing lives in people.
In the gurdwara, the singers of kirtan are called ragis, and their craft passes from teacher to student.
Some ragis and teachers give their lives to singing each shabad in the raga its heading names, often with stringed instruments as well as harmonium and tabla.
This way of singing is often called Gurmat Sangeet, the music of the Guru's way, and there are schools and teachers devoted to keeping it.
In other gurdwaras and homes, shabads are sung to simpler tunes a whole congregation can pick up.
Sikhs hold different views about how closely kirtan should follow the named raga, and the singing goes on both ways, sometimes in the same building on the same day. What both share is the text.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada, in paraphrase, says that in the congregation kirtan is the singing of Gurbani, with only certain other writings allowed beside it.

teach.h: THE WORDS STAY; THE TUNE IS HANDED DOWN.
teach.b: The words don't change; the tune is the part handed down by ear.
So the raga names on this road aren't museum labels. Somewhere a student may be learning Prabhati for a morning program, and a ragi tuning up for Kalyan at dusk.

how: In gurdwaras, ragis lead kirtan with harmonium and tabla, and some also use stringed instruments and sing each shabad in the raga named in its heading; congregations also sing shabads to simpler tunes everyone can join.

o: a new style of kirtan written in the last century
old recordings of kirtan kept in a museum archive

games.q: you're a young ragi with a shabad headed Raag Prabhati. the page names the raga but gives no notes. where do you learn the tune?
o: from a teacher, voice to voice.
you make up anything you like.
games.why: the craft is passed from teacher to student by ear, like a recipe learned at the stove.

practice: If you can, search for one shabad sung in the raga its heading names, adding raag kirtan or Gurmat Sangeet to the search, and as it plays, sit still and notice how the voice and the instruments move together, letting the breath follow the music's pace.

If you can't play anything, recall a melody you learned from a person rather than a screen. If you pray, listen as kirtan is meant to be heard, as Gurbani sung; if you don't, simply listen like someone being taught.
